title: Coaching Case Studies #1
author: Craig Barton
summary: Barton applies the instructional coaching process he set out the previous week to two teachers in a Midlands maths department, and writes the sessions up as worked examples. In the first, a colleague wanted to improve questioning during the Do Now; Barton's hypothesis was that the ten-minute starter was being consumed by books, pens, date and title, and his critical evidence was an exercise book containing a copied date and nothing else. The redesign is specific: three minutes on a visible timer for equipment and heading, then one question at a time projected with roughly twenty seconds of thinking and a mini-whiteboard show, producing a whole-class check on both effort and understanding. In the second, a colleague worried that a low-attaining Year 7 class did not follow his explanations; Barton observed a five-minute uninterrupted explanation on linear sequences, noted students looking out of the window and doodling, and gathered one student's failed follow-up question as evidence. The remedy was to chunk the explanation and check after each chunk by Cold Call or whiteboard, then to script and rehearse the exact wording — reproduced in the post as a dialogue. What makes the piece useful is the visible coaching mechanics: a hypothesis about something the teacher cannot see, a single piece of critical evidence, then a rehearsed change.
points: The coaching method on display is the transferable part — form a hypothesis about what the teacher cannot see, then hunt for one piece of critical evidence that settles it.
A photographed exercise book showing ten minutes of work amounting to a copied date does more persuasive work than any lesson-observation judgement.
The Do Now redesign separates admin time from thinking time with a timer, then paces the questioning one item at a time so non-participation becomes visible.
Barton's second case treats a five-minute unbroken explanation as a design fault rather than an attention problem, fixed by chunking and checking after each chunk.
Scripting and rehearsing the teacher's actual words — including the response to a student who says 'no idea' — is what turns coaching advice into next-day practice.
quotes: Last week I wrote about how I approach instructional coaching. On Thursday I was lucky enough to put this process into practice when I worked with lovely colleagues from a maths department in the Midlands.

My hypothesis during those first 10 minutes was that by the time the teacher started going through the answers, many of the students would not have thought about some, or even any, of the questions. My critical evidence was books like this, where after 10 minutes the date was copied down and nothing more.

During the coaching session, we worked on a different model for the Do Now. Students would be given 3 minutes to get their books and pens out, and copy the date and title (there would be a timer on the board for added impetus). After the 3 minutes were up, the teacher would begin the Do Now, but only project one question on the board.

This gives a whole-class check for both effort and understanding and is the kind of pacier Do Now where students cannot get away with doing nothing. Having gauged understanding, the teacher could respond accordingly, either by moving on, calling upon students to explain their reasoning, or modelling and providing a subsequent follow-up question.

I watched an explanation on generating terms of linear sequences that lasted about five minutes and quickly concluded that many students were not listening. Some were looking out of the window, others were doodling in their books. My hypothesis was that students would not be able to complete the question that followed the explanation.

During the coaching session, we discussed breaking explanations down into much shorter chunks, and following each chunk up with a check for effort and understanding. This check could be a Cold Call directed at a specific student, or it could be a whole-class check using mini-whiteboards.
